Text 1
The industrialist Dmitri Colombo funded the construction of the Thornbridge Free Library, celebrated for making scientific periodicals available to working-class readers in the 1880s. Not all of Colombo's actions were admirable, however. Most notoriously, he orchestrated a six-month lockout against the ironworkers' association at his foundry, even withholding nearly 8,000 dollars in wages that arbitrators later ruled had already been earned. So Colombo's legacy should be regarded as dubious at best.

Text 2
Some historians, such as Chinwe Dlamini, argue that Colombo's harsh treatment of his workers is as central to his biography as his civic philanthropy. But his lockout at the foundry must be understood as an indirect consequence of a contractual dispute over a revised piecework schedule: he was enforcing terms he believed the existing agreement permitted.
prompt: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the claim in the underlined sentence in Text 1?

choices.A: By suggesting that whatever offenses Colombo might have committed are outweighed by the civic value of the Thornbridge Free Library.
choices.B: By agreeing that though his contracts may have permitted Colombo to do so, Colombo was wrong to have locked out the ironworkers.
choices.C: By pointing out that if Colombo had taken the actions of which he is accused, then there would be documentation of those actions in the records of the Thornbridge Free Library.
choices.D: By asserting that an evaluation of Colombo's conduct should take into account that he believed his actions were justified.

explanation:
Choice D is the best answer. Text 1 concludes in the underlined sentence that Colombo's legacy should be regarded as 'dubious at best' because of the lockout and withheld wages. The author of Text 2 acknowledges that Colombo's harsh treatment of workers is central to his biography but qualifies the judgment by arguing the lockout was an 'indirect consequence of a contractual dispute' and that Colombo was 'enforcing terms he believed the existing agreement permitted.' Text 2 would therefore respond by asserting that any evaluation of Colombo's conduct should account for his belief that his actions were justified.

Why B is incorrect:

Choice B is incorrect because it mischaracterizes Text 2's position. Text 2 does not agree that Colombo was wrong to lock out the ironworkers; rather, it contextualizes his actions by noting they arose from a contractual dispute and that he believed the existing agreement permitted his conduct. Text 2 offers no moral judgment that the action itself was wrong.
